extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO officials, policymakers, and patent litigators
extracted.subtask_short: US patent reform statutes and procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of substantive standards and procedural rules in the Patent Reform Act of 2007, covering damages, willful infringement, post-grant review (PGR) procedures, venue, PTO authority, inequitable conduct, applicant obligations, and related PTO/Board structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty methods (A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The contribution of the claimed invention over the prior art is the predominant basis for the market demand of the larger apparatus/process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as one method for calculating a reasonable royalty (subsection A). The text positions the claimed invention's contribution over the prior art as a primary driver of the infringing product's market demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty methods (B) - Established marketplace royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Established royalty based on marketplace licensing--the royalty may be based on other nonexclusive licenses of the patented invention if the claimed invention has been the subject of a nonexclusive license to a number of persons sufficient to indicate a general marketplace recognition of the reasonableness of the licensing terms, if the license was secured prior to the filing of the case, and if the infringer’s use is of substantially the same scope, volume and benefit of the rights granted under such license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may rely on pre-existing nonexclusive licenses as a basis for reasonable royalty when licences demonstrate marketplace recognition and are comparable in scope/volume/benefit and were secured prior to filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty methods (C) - Apportionment to claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If showings under (A) and (B) have not been made, the court shall conduct an analysis to ensure that a reasonable royalty is applied only to the portion of the economic value of the infringing product or process properly attributable to the claimed invention’s specific contribution over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires apportionment: royalty must be limited to the economic value specifically attributable to the claimed invention over the prior art (avoid applying royalty to value from unclaimed/known features).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination invention valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of a combination invention whose elements are present individually in the prior art, the contribution over the prior art may include the value of the additional function resulting from the combination, as well as the enhanced value, if any, of some or all of the prior art elements as part of the combination, if the patentee demonstrates that value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owner may show value arising from new function produced by the combination and/or enhancement of prior-art elements as part of apportionment for reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of other relevant factors in reasonable royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining a reasonable royalty, where appropriate, the court may also consider (or direct the jury to consider) any other relevant factors under applicable law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-exhaustive: courts retain discretion to consider other legally relevant Georgia-Pacific-type factors or others as appropriate; methods in subsection apply only to reasonable-royalty damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement—damages increase and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may increase damages by up to three times based on a finding of willful infringement. A determination of willful infringement shall be made without a jury. To prove willful infringement, a patentee must prove by clear and convincing evidence one of specified conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willfulness increases damages up to treble; trial judge (not jury) decides willfulness; patentee bears clear-and-convincing burden and must meet one of the enumerated factual routes (notice+continued infringement; intentional copying; repeat infringer behavior after court finding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness route (A) - detailed written notice and continued infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The infringer received written notice from the patentee (i) alleging acts of infringement in a manner sufficient to give the infringer an objectively reasonable apprehension of suit on such patent, and (ii) identifying with particularity each claim of the patent, each allegedly infringing product or process, and the relationship of such product or process to such claim, the infringer, after a reasonable opportunity to investigate, thereafter performed one or more acts of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice must be particularized (claims, accused products/processes, claim-to-product relationship); continued acts after reasonable opportunity to investigate constitutes willfulness element A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness route (B) - intentional copying
rubrics_metrics.description: After receiving such notice and after a reasonable opportunity to investigate, the infringer intentionally copied the patented invention with knowledge that it was patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires proof of intentional copying coupled with knowledge of patent; follows notice and investigation opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness route (C) - repeat non-colorably-different conduct after adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: After having been found by a court to infringe a patent, the infringer engaged in conduct that was not colorably different from the conduct previously found to have infringed the patent, and which resulted in a separate finding of infringement of the same patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post‑adjudication repetition of substantially identical conduct that leads to additional infringement findings qualifies as willfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement limitations — good faith defense
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may not find that an infringer has willfully infringed a patent for any period of time during which the infringer had an informed good faith belief that the patent was invalid or unenforceable, or would not be infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'informed good faith belief' may be established by (a) reasonable reliance on advice of counsel; (b) evidence that the infringer sought to modify its conduct to avoid infringement once it had discovered the patent; or (c) other evidence a court may find sufficient. Decision not to present advice-of-counsel evidence is not relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement limitations — pleading timing
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may not plead (and a court may not determine) willful infringement before the date on which a court determines that the patent in suit is not invalid, is enforceable, and has been infringed by the infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should not determine willfulness before threshold rulings on validity, enforceability, and infringement are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user rights study requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 2 years from the date of enactment, the Director shall report to Congress his findings and recommendations regarding the operation of 'prior user rights' in selected countries as compared to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative directive to study international prior-user-rights regimes and report recommendations to Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking and notice — limitation on past damages
rubrics_metrics.description: For patented inventions not covered under subsection (a)(1), past damages shall be limited to 2 years prior to the filing of a complaint (or counterclaim) except upon proof that the infringer was notified of infringement by the patentee. In no case shall liability for past damages exceed 6 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caps retrospective damages window at 2 years unless patentee can prove notice; absolute maximum of 6 years for past damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user rights affiliates
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (b)(6) of Sec. 273 is amended to also allow 'affiliates' of the person who performed the necessary prior user rights acts to assert the defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expands availability of prior-user defense to affiliated entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of Post-Grant Review (PGR) and filing windows
rubrics_metrics.description: Creates a new post-grant review proceeding that allows third parties to petition the USPTO to review patents that may be invalid. There are two 'windows' for filing: 1st window petitions must be filed within 1 year of the patent issuing; 2nd window petitions may be filed at any time after the patent issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR is a new administrative route to challenge patents at the PTO with distinct timing windows and differing procedures/standards where specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeal of inter partes reexamination and amendments to Sec.303
rubrics_metrics.description: In view of the creation of this new PGR system, Sec. 303(a) is amended and inter partes reexamination is repealed. Within three months of a request for reexamination by the patent owner, or at any time on the Director’s own initiative, the Director may determine whether a substantial new question of patentability is raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replaces previous inter partes reexamination mechanism with PGR and gives Director certain screening timeframe/authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.321 — Petition for post-grant review permissible grounds and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Permits a 3rd party to file a PGR petition with the PTO to cancel a claim as invalid based on any ground that might be raised under Sec. 282(b)(2) and (3). The Director shall establish fees to be paid by the person requesting the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR petitions may assert statutory invalidity grounds; participation requires fee set by Director.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.322 — Timing and basis of PGR petition (three circumstances)
rubrics_metrics.description: A PGR petition may be filed in any one of three circumstances: (1) within 12 months of the patent’s issuance or reissuance (1st window); (2)(i) substantial reason to believe continued existence of the challenged claim is likely to cause the petitioner significant economic harm, and (ii) the petitioner files within 12 months after receiving notice (explicitly or implicitly) of infringement; or (3) the patent owner consents (2 and 3 are 2nd window).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines narrow 1st window and broader 2nd-window paths tied to economic harm/notice or owner consent; each path has distinct predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.323 — Requirements of petition
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition must, inter alia, include the necessary fee, identify the real parties in interest, specifically identify each claim challenged, the grounds for challenging it, and the evidence that supports each challenge, including, where applicable, copies of relevant patents and printed publications, or supporting affidavits or declarations. The Director may, by regulation, require additional information. The petitioner must provide a copy of the petition with supporting documents to the patent owner or his designated representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions must be detailed and supported by evidence; service on patent owner required; Director can require more info.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.324 — Publication and public availability of petition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director shall publish the petition in the Federal Register and make that petition available on the USPTO website. Any PGR file shall be made available to the public unless a petition or document is accompanied with a motion to seal. Such petition or document shall be treated as sealed, pending outcome of ruling on the motion. Failure to file motion to seal will result in the pleading being placed in the public record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default is public disclosure of petitions; sealing is possible only with motion and pending ruling; publication in Federal Register and USPTO site is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.325 — Prohibited filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive petitions under any subsection of Sec. 322, filed by the same party on the same patent, are prohibited. A PGR proceeding may not be instituted or maintained under paragraph (1) or (2) of Sec. 322 if the petitioner or real party in interest has instituted a civil action challenging the validity of a claim of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents serial petitions by same party on same patent and bars certain PGRs where litigation challenging the same claim has been filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.326 — Submission of additional information
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner shall file such additional information as the Director may require by regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Director may impose further documentary/pleading requirements; petitioners must comply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.327 — Institution standard and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may not authorize a PGR proceeding to commence unless the Director determines that the information presented in the petition raises a substantial new question of patentability for at least one of the challenged claims. The Director shall decide a petition within 90 days of its receipt, notify the petitioner and patent owner, and if granted shall publish notice including the date the PGR proceeding shall commence. The determination is not appealable. The Director shall assign a PGR proceeding to a panel of 3 Board judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-level screening standard: 'substantial new question of patentability' required; 90-day decision clock; institution decisions are final (nonappealable); assigned to three-judge panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.328 — Consolidation and joinder
rubrics_metrics.description: If more than one petition is submitted under Sec. 322(1) against the same patent and each raises a substantial new question, the Director may consolidate such proceedings. If the Director commences a PGR on basis of a petition under Sec.322(2), any person who files in compliance with section 322(2)(A) a petition that the Director finds sufficient may be joined at the Director's discretion, and such person shall participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Director has discretion to consolidate multiple institution-worthy petitions and to join additional 2nd-window petitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.329 — Regulations governing PGR conduct and discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director shall prescribe regulations establishing and governing PGR proceedings and their relationship to other proceedings. Regulations shall set standards for showings of substantial reason to believe and significant economic harm and substantial new question; provide for publication of requests for institution; establish supplemental-information submission procedures; set discovery procedures; require final determination no later than 1 year after institution (extendable up to 6 months for good cause); provide for discovery upon order of the Director as required in interests of justice; prescribe sanctions for abuse; provide protective orders for confidential information; and ensure information submitted by patent owner in support of any amendment is made public as part of prosecution history. In prescribing regulations, Director shall consider the effect on the economy, integrity of the patent system, and efficient administration of the Office. The PTAB shall conduct each proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive regulatory framework: sets timing limits (1 year + 6 months), discovery scope (Director-ordered), sanctions, confidentiality protections, and public-record rules for amendment-supporting submissions; Director must consider systemic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.330 — Patent owner response rights in PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: After a PGR proceeding has been instituted, the patent owner shall have the right to file a timely response, which may include affidavits, declarations and any additional factual evidence and expert opinions on which the patent owner relies in support of the response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owners may fully respond with factual and expert evidence once PGR instituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.331 — Evidentiary standards and burden in PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption of validity set forth in Sec. 282 shall not apply to challenges brought under Sec. 322(1) but shall apply in a challenge brought under paragraph (2) or (3) of Sec. 322. The petitioner under Sec.322(1) shall have the burden of proving invalidity by a preponderance of the evidence. For petitions under 322(2) or (3), existence/authentication/availability/scope of any evidence offered to establish invalidity shall be established by clear and convincing evidence; if such predicate facts are so established, invalidity shall be proven only if the persuasive force of such facts demonstrates invalidity by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different evidentiary regimes: first-window (322(1)) challenges proceed without the presumption of validity and require preponderance; second-window (322(2)/(3)) challenges preserve presumption and impose a two-step predicate (clear-and-convincing factual predicate then preponderance for legal conclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.332 — Patent owner amendment in PGR (limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: During a PGR, the patent owner may file one motion to amend the patent in one or more ways: (1) cancel any challenged claim; (2) propose a substitute claim for each challenged claim; or (3) amend the patent drawings or otherwise amend the patent other than the claims. Additional motions permitted only for good cause. An amendment may not enlarge the scope of the claims or introduce new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrow amendment rights: single primary motion allowed; no enlargement of claim scope or new matter permitted; additional motions require good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.333 — Settlement and estoppel consequences in PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: A PGR shall be terminated with respect to any petitioner upon joint request of the petitioner and patent owner unless the Office has decided the matter before the request. If terminated with respect to a petitioner under this section, no estoppel under this chapter shall apply to that petitioner. If no petitioner remains, Office shall terminate the PGR. Any agreement to terminate must be in writing and a true copy filed in the USPTO; on request, copy may be kept separate and made available only to Federal Government agencies upon written request or to any other person on showing of good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement can terminate a petitioner's participation without triggering statutory estoppel, but written filing requirements exist and limited confidentiality options are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.334 — Final written decision by the Board
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proceeding is not otherwise dismissed, the Patent Board shall issue a final written decision with respect to the patentability of any patent claim challenged and any new claim added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB will render a final written decision addressing challenged (and any substitute) claims at end of PGR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.335 — Effect of Board decision on patent record
rubrics_metrics.description: If a final decision of the Board that is not timely appealed (or if that appeal is terminated), the Director shall publish a certificate canceling any claim determined unpatentable, and shall incorporate in the patent any new claim determined to be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final PTAB decisions are implemented by certificate changing the patent's claims (cancellation/incorporation) when not appealed or appeal resolved against appellant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.337 — Effect of civil-action decisions on future PGR requests
rubrics_metrics.description: If a final decision has been entered against a party in a civil action arising under section 1338 establishing that the party has not sustained its burden of proving the invalidity of any patent claim, that party may not subsequently request a PGR on that patent claim on the basis of any grounds under Sec.322. In addition, the Director may not subsequently maintain a PGR previously requested by that party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adverse civil-action final decisions preclude same party from later pursuing PGR on same grounds; Director must decline/terminate overlapping PGRs by that party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.338 — Collateral effects of favorable PGR final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: If a final decision under Sec.334 is favorable to the patentability of any original or new claim of the patent challenged by the petitioner, the petitioner may not thereafter, based on any ground which the petitioner raised during the PGR, (1) request or pursue a derivation proceeding with respect to such claim; or (2) assert the invalidity of any such claim in any civil action arising in whole or in part under section 1338. If final decision results from a petition filed on basis of Sec.322(2), the prohibition extends to any ground the petitioner raised during the PGR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful defense at PTAB creates estoppel preventing petitioner from later raising same grounds in derivation or civil actions (with extended scope for certain 2nd-window petitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.339 — Appeal rights from PGR final determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: A party dissatisfied with the final determination of the Board in a PGR proceeding may appeal the determinations under Secs.141 through 144. Any party to the PGR proceeding shall have the right to be a party to the appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard appeal route to the Federal Circuit via statutory appeal provisions; all PGR parties have right to be parties to appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.6 — Creation and responsibilities of the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences is replaced with the new Patent Trial and Appeal Board ('Board'). The Board is charged with (i) reviewing adverse decisions of examiners on applications and reexamination proceedings, (ii) conducting derivation proceedings, and (iii) conducting the post-grant review proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural change: PTAB consolidates appeals, derivation, and PGR functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.7 — Third-party pre-issuance submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Creates a mechanism in Sec.122 for third parties to submit timely pre-issuance information relevant to the examination of the application, including a concise statement of the relevance of the submission. Also repeals exception to the 18-month publication requirement for applicants not filing abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third parties may feed relevant prior art/information to examiners during examination with a required concise relevance statement; publication rules adjusted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.8 — Venue for patent infringement civil actions (amended 1400(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil actions for patent infringement, including declaratory judgment actions, may only be brought in a judicial district (1) where the defendant has its principal place of business or is incorporated or formed, or, for a foreign corporation with a U.S. subsidiary, where its primary U.S. subsidiary has its principal place of business or is incorporated or formed; (2) where the defendant has committed substantial acts of infringement and has a regular and established physical facility that the defendant controls and that constitutes a substantial portion of the operations of the defendant; (3) where the primary plaintiff resides, if the primary plaintiff is an institution of higher education or a nonprofit patent and licensing organization; (4) where the plaintiff resides, if the sole plaintiff is an individual inventor who qualifies as a 'micro-entity' pursuant to section 123 of title 35.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrows venue to districts having a direct relation to defendant or to certain plaintiff residencies; seeks to limit forum shopping by requiring meaningful ties to the chosen forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.8 — Transfer and interlocutory appeal procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may request transfer where (1) parties have substantial evidence or witnesses that otherwise would present considerable evidentiary burdens to the defendant if such transfer were not granted, (2) transfer would not cause undue hardship to the plaintiff, and (3) venue would be otherwise appropriate under section 1391. Interlocutory appeals: Federal Circuit to accept all interlocutory appeals of claim construction orders when certified by the district court; party wishing to appeal must file a motion within 10 days; district court has discretion whether to certify and whether to stay proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets transfer criteria to protect defendants from unfair forum choice and facilitates interlocutory Federal Circuit review of claim construction when certified by district court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.9 — PTO rulemaking authority over fees and consultation/notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Gives the Director rulemaking authority to set or adjust any fee under Secs.41 and 376 and section 1113 of title 15, provided such fee amounts are set to reasonably compensate the USPTO for the services performed. The Director may also reduce such fees. The Director shall consult with the patent and trademark advisory committees. Any proposal for a change in fees (including rationale/purpose/possible expectations or benefits) shall be published in the Federal Register and seek public comment for at least 45 days. The Director shall notify Congress of any final proposed fee change and Congress shall have up to 45 days to consider and comment before the change becomes effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Director has broad fee-setting authority subject to consultation, public notice, comment, and congressional notification periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.11 — Applicant quality submissions and mandatory applicant obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sec.123 added to provide the Director authority to promulgate rules that require a patent applicant to submit a search report and analysis relevant to patentability and other relevant information as determined by the Director. Failure to comply with such requirements shall result in abandonment of the application. A 'micro-entity' is exempt from this requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential new applicant duty to provide prior-art search/analysis under Director rules; noncompliance can cause abandonment; micro-entities exempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.12 — Inequitable conduct standard (Sec.298)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party asserting that a patent should be cancelled or held unenforceable due to inequitable conduct shall prove independently, by clear and convincing evidence, that material information was misrepresented, or omitted, from the patent application with the intention of deceiving the USPTO. Information is material if a reasonable examiner would consider such information important in deciding whether to allow the patent application; any such information is not cumulative. Although intent to deceive may be inferred, it may not be done so based solely on the gross negligence of the patent owner or its representative, or on the materiality of the information misrepresented or not disclosed. The party asserting the defense shall comply with the pleading requirements set forth under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 9(b). If the court finds inequitable conduct, the court has discretion to (1) hold the entire patent unenforceable, (2) hold one or more claims unenforceable, or (3) hold that patentee is not entitled to an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elevates and clarifies the elements (materiality + intent) and pleading standard for inequitable-conduct claims; bars inferring intent from mere gross negligence or materiality alone; provides remedies and requires FRCP 9(b) particularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.13 — Director authority to accept late filings for unintentional delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Director may accept a late filing if the applicant or owner (i) files a petition within 30 days after the missed deadline, and (ii) demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Director the delay was unintentional. The petition shall be deemed denied if the Director has not made a determination within 60 days after its filing. Director’s decisions on such petitions shall not be subject to judicial review. This subsection shall not apply to other provisions that allow the Director to accept late filings, or to treaty-required statutory deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates a discrete 30-day petition mechanism for unintentional delay with 60-day decision timeline and no judicial review of Director's decision; limited in scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.14 — Limitation on remedies for check imaging methods used by financial institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Amends Sec.287 to provide that use by a financial institution of a check collection system that constitutes infringement under section 271 shall not trigger the provisions of sections 281, 283, 284, and 285 against the financial institution. Definitions provided for 'check,' 'check collection system,' 'financial institution,' 'substitute check,' and 'truncate.' Applies to any civil action pending or filed on or after enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carves out remedies against financial institutions using certain check-imaging systems; statutory definitions and retroactive application to pending/future civil actions specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.15 — PTO funding and financial oversight requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminates appropriation of USPTO fees and establishes a revolving fund in the Treasury; all fees collected deposited and available until expended. Director shall submit an annual report to Congress within 60 days after fiscal year end; notify Congress the Office’s annual spending plan within 30 days after beginning of each fiscal year; provide for an independent audit annually in accordance with generally acceptable accounting procedures; fund to prepare and submit each year to the President a business-type budget per section 9301 of title 31.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts PTO finance to a fee-funded revolving model with annual reporting, spending-plan notice, independent audits, and budget submission obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.16 — Technical amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Sets forth technical amendments consistent with this Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placeholder for conforming/technical statutory edits accompanying substantive changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec.17 — Effective date and rule of construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as otherwise provided, this Act takes effect 12 months after enactment and applies to any patent issued on or after that effective date. Special administration guidance: enactment of Sec.102(b)(3) is to be administered consistent with CREATE Act intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General effective-date rule with transitional provisions for patents issued on/after the effective date and treatment consistent with prior cooperative-research administration (CREATE Act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue statutory history and rationale guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of history of venue statute (28 U.S.C. 1400(b)), Supreme Court decisions, Federal Circuit VE Holding, and the need to limit forum shopping by narrowing venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides legislative and policy rationale for amending venue: to prevent forum shopping, preserve uniform national patent law, reduce inappropriate pressure to settle, and locate litigation where evidence/witnesses relate to the dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data on forum-shopping consequences and empirical findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence cited (studies, district statistics) indicating concentration of patent suits in certain districts and resulting forum-shopping effects, supporting venue reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualizes venue reform with statistics and studies (e.g., district filing rates, plaintiff success rates) illustrating the practical problem the statute seeks to remedy.
